name: Nora Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. This interview is confidential. What does an ordinary day at the contact centre look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 43 and lead the complaints queue at a contact centre. My two-year college diploma was in office administration, and I have become the person other agents call when a payment is posted to the wrong customer. I am good at the work and earn the usual wage for it. I never use AI tools; I read the ledger and the customer’s words.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of a day do you remember at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Amir and I have two children in school and a mortgage. He maintains the local library building, and we have about four months of expenses saved. There are some other centres within reach, although a new job still means a new rota. I remember the customer who had to call three times for a payment we could have corrected on the first call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my team AI Plateau is no excuse to shorten the time we spend finding a wrong payment. I would ask the staff meeting to put proper correction time back on the rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job stays and four months saved gives us some room. I still dislike a target that praises a closed ticket when the customer’s balance is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep leading complaints and bring three repeated payment cases to the staff meeting. In the first year of minor change, I’d join colleagues in a written request for paid correction time on the rota while keeping our savings for the mortgage and repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about my wage, irritated by the ticket target. A customer should not need a fourth phone call to get one payment moved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which cases would you bring?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use the case where the same transfer appeared on two accounts. The customer had all the receipts, but each short call ended before anyone compared them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the reserve for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Amir (my partner) and I keep the reserve in a plain savings account. We can pay for a broken boiler, but I will not spend that buffer on a new screen.

say: I’d defend **time to correct payments** instead of chasing closed tickets.
I’d ask colleagues to demand **paid correction time** on the rota.
think: I think my **job remains** in this mild picture.
I value our **four-month reserve** for repairs and the mortgage.
do: Keep **leading complaints** and bring three repeated payment cases to the staff meeting in 2026.
Join colleagues’ **written demand** for paid correction time on the rota in the first year.
feel: **Calm** about wages, irritated by bad targets.

fieldNote: Her **four-month cushion** absorbs an ordinary repair.

The repeated **payment case** gives her group evidence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption will remove ordinary chat answers before the complaints pile disappears. I would join colleagues in asking for written paid hours, appeal rights and a person authorised to correct wrong balances.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could still handle disputes, but the centre might staff fewer agents to do them. Four months saved is helpful, yet a smaller wage would make the mortgage harder every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d help send the group’s written demand for appeal hours and keep doing the ledger checks myself. In the first year routine chats move, I’d apply for a posted paid complaints role at another nearby centre only if its written weekly wage and hours cover our mortgage; I would stay here until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the rota, not curious about the software. A half-empty call queue can still leave a full mortgage payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which hours would you ask for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for the paid appeal hours by shift. A total number of answered chats hides who was taken off the rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your partner check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask Amir (my partner) to look at the whole week of pay, not just the hourly rate. We have the school run to fit around it too.

say: I’d ask for **written appeal hours** with colleagues.
I’d demand a **paid human correction route** for wrong balances.
think: I think my **dispute skill** may still be needed.
I fear **fewer paid shifts** would strain the mortgage despite savings.
do: Join the **group appeal-hours demand** and keep checking ledgers myself in 2026.
Apply for **posted nearby complaints work** only with written mortgage-covering weekly pay and hours fitting school runs; stay until signed offer.
S1.quote: A half-empty call queue can still leave a full mortgage payment.
fieldNote: She separates **case volume** from paid staff hours.
She checks **full-week pay** and school runs before moving.
Her **moderate reserve** buys time but cannot replace wages indefinitely.

steps.text: Join colleagues demanding written paid appeal hours and correction authority
Keep checking customer payment ledgers personally

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team AGI by 2028 could make the complaints decision as well as the first reply. I would join a written demand for notice and a paid human route to reverse wrong balances.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my best work may vanish with the routine calls in 2028. Robots around 2031 are later and do not delay the risk to a headset; four months saved is a bridge, not a replacement income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d help colleagues demand written staffing notice and paid appeal hours, and postpone the planned patio paving while the surface remains safe. In the first year after 2028, I’d apply for a posted paid hospital-admissions role only if its written weekly wage and hours cover our mortgage and fit school pickups, keeping this job until a signed offer; I’d take a required admissions course only if funded on paid time for that vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, even with some savings. Four months of savings is enough to look for work, not enough to wait for an entire occupation to reappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the patio?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Amir (my partner) the patio can wait unless the loose slab becomes a trip hazard. Then we would repair that slab, not pay for a whole new surface.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What terms would make the course possible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask to see the posted vacancy, the paid study hours and the first week’s rota. I will not use mortgage savings on a course that merely might lead to work.

say: I’d warn that **2028 AGI** may take the whole complaints decision before staff can prepare.
I’d join a **notice-and-appeals demand** with colleagues.
think: I think my **best desk work** could vanish in 2028.
I see **four months saved** as a short bridge, not wages.
do: Join the **group notice demand** and defer safe patio paving in 2026.
Apply for **posted admissions work** after 2028 only with written mortgage-covering weekly pay and school-compatible hours; stay until signed offer.
Take a **required admissions course** only if funded on paid time for that posted paid vacancy.
S2.quote: Four months of savings is enough to look for work, not enough to wait for an entire occupation to reappear.
fieldNote: She treats **2028 thinking AI** as the immediate risk.
The **patio delay** stops if a slab becomes unsafe.
A course requires **paid funded time** and a posted vacancy.

steps.text: Join colleagues demanding written staffing notice and paid appeal hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives us time to insist that any new role is a real paid vacancy. I would join a staff request for funded admissions training on paid time and written appeal hours while the old desk still operates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could learn the hospital’s admission rules if someone teaches them properly, though full AGI may also handle forms. I will not start an unpaid course while our mortgage still comes each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2026 I’d join the group demand and take a funded admissions course on paid time only if a posted paid vacancy requires it. In the first year after 2031, I’d apply for that role only if its written weekly wage and hours cover the mortgage and let us collect the children from school, keeping my current job until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but the extra years let me check the actual rota. A classroom seat is not a shift on the payroll.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should training include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want to practise correcting a mistaken patient address with an experienced admissions worker. A rulebook alone will not show who is allowed to change the record.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the family check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the family to compare the school timetable with both work rotas. A better rate means little if we have to pay for care every afternoon.

I’d ask for **written appeal hours** at the current desk.
think: I think I could learn **admissions rules** with proper teaching.
I doubt **unpaid study** fits our mortgage or the children’s school timetable.
do: Join the **staff training demand** and take required funded admissions training on paid time for a posted paid vacancy.
Apply for **posted admissions work** after 2031 only with written mortgage-covering weekly pay and school-compatible hours; stay until signed offer.
Compare the **school timetable** with both work rotas and account for any extra childcare costs before accepting.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to check real terms.
S3.quote: A classroom seat is not a shift on the payroll.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 gives us a decade to keep the right to correct a wrong payment in paid hands. I would join colleagues in asking for the appeal rota and correction authority in writing each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I can earn and keep our reserve healthy for years, although full thinking AI may still take complaints in 2036. Robots around 2039 do not protect the calls I answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep leading complaints, add a fixed amount from each pay to our reserve and join the annual group demand for paid appeal hours. In the first year after 2036, I’d apply for posted paid customer-account work only if my hours fall and its written weekly wage and school-compatible hours cover our mortgage, keeping this job until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about 2036, calm enough about next year to plan. Ten years before AGI gives me time to choose a route without spending the mortgage buffer on a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check annually?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the paid correction hours with reopened payment cases every spring. If cases rise while hours fall, the group has a concrete reason to demand more time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move the family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the children at their school unless Amir (my partner) and I had a signed offer with enough pay after travel and housing costs. Some nearby centres let us search without moving first.

say: I’d demand **paid appeal hours** and correction authority with colleagues each year.
I’d keep **wrong-payment reversals** available to customers.
think: I think I can **work and save** for years.
I know **2036 thinking AI** could still take my complaints desk.
do: Keep **leading complaints**, save from each pay and join yearly group demands for paid appeal hours.
Apply for **posted account work** after 2036 if hours fall, with written mortgage-covering wage and school-compatible hours; stay until signed offer.
Relocate the family only with a **signed offer** leaving enough after travel and housing costs; preserve the children’s school where possible.
feel: **Uneasy** about 2036, calm about the near term.
S4.quote: Ten years before AGI gives me time to choose a route without spending the mortgage buffer on a guess.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because a four-month reserve would run down before I knew whether paid complaints work still exists. I would want written staffing notice and a shared agreement that customers can reach a paid appeal agent. A posted paid role with written mortgage-covering weekly hours and wage would make a move possible; I would only take required training if it were funded on paid time.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask how a customer gets the electricity money back after a wrong payment. Somebody needs both authority and paid hours to reverse a wrong electricity payment.

headlineQuote: Somebody needs both authority and paid hours to reverse a wrong electricity payment.
portrait: At **43**, Nora leads hard complaints after a two-year college diploma on typical pay.
She and Amir support **two schoolchildren** and a mortgage with four months saved.
She avoids **AI tools** and checks payment ledgers herself.
She seeks **written appeal rights** and real paid jobs before changing her work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could erase paid complaints work before four months of savings buys another job.
whatWouldHelp: **Written staffing notice**, shared paid appeals and a posted mortgage-covering role with funded required training would help.
